summary: Defines an extension to the Extensible Provisioning Protocol that lets registrars ask a registry what fees and credits apply to billable actions and state the expected fees when issuing commands. It exists because new domain extensions and business models have made pricing more varied.

plainLanguage.summary: Before buying something, you ask the shop its price and say what you expect to pay. This lets domain sellers do that with registries.

questions: how do epp clients query domain fees
what is the epp fee extension
how are refundable fees marked in epp
what is the grace period for a domain fee
subtitle: Let registries tell clients what domain operations will cost.

tldr.problem: Domain registries have grown and charge varied fees for operations on different domain extensions and classes. Registrars had no standard way to learn fees from a registry before committing to an operation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8748 adds an extension to the Extensible Provisioning Protocol that lets registrars query a registry for fees and credits associated with domain creation, renewal, transfer and other billable operations, and declare expected fees when issuing commands.
tldr.outcome: Registries and registrars can now coordinate on pricing without out-of-band contact, supporting complex fee structures for new domain extensions and business models.

facts.label: Supported commands
facts.value: create, delete, renew, update, transfer, restore

facts.label: Currency codes
facts.value: ISO 4217 (USD, EUR) or XXX for non-currency

today: RFC 8748 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2020 and has not been obsoleted or updated. The fee extension is widely implemented by domain registries and is used to handle complex pricing for new domain extensions and premium domains.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Historically, domain name registries applied a simple fee structure: a single price for domain creation, renewal, transfer, and grace-period restore operations. With the expansion of the DNS namespace and new domain extensions (TLDs like .crypto, .xyz), registries now offer tiered pricing, premium names, and variable rates.

Before this RFC, registrars had no standard way to learn what fees a registry would charge for a given domain or operation. They had to contact registry operators out of band to discover fees. RFC 8748 fixes this by adding a fee extension to the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP), the standard protocol for managing domain registrations.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet had lots of different kinds of domains with different prices, and nobody had agreed on how to ask a registry what each one cost. This RFC is the agreement.

sections.title: How the Fee Extension Works
sections.content:
The extension adds new elements to EPP commands and responses. When a registrar wants to know a domain's fees, it sends a fee check command: a query that names a domain, a command (like create or renew), and optionally a currency code and registration period. The registry responds with the fees and credits for that domain and operation.

For example, a registrar can query the fee for creating example.com for 2 years in USD. The registry responds with the fee amount, whether it is refundable (for instance, during a grace period after deletion), and the grace period duration. The registrar can also state expected fees in transform commands (create, renew, delete, transfer, update), and the server validates them before applying charges.
sections.plainLanguage: The registrar asks 'how much to register example.com for 2 years?', and the registry says '5 dollars, and you get it back if you delete within 5 days'.

sections.title: Fee Elements and Data Structures
sections.content:
The extension defines elements for queries and responses. The fee check element contains one or more <fee:command> elements, each specifying an operation name (create, delete, renew, update, transfer, restore, or custom) and an optional period. The registry response includes a fee check data element with one <fee:cd> (check data) element per queried domain.

Each check-data element contains one <fee:command> per queried command, which holds zero or more <fee:fee> elements (debits) and <fee:credit> elements (credits). Fees can carry attributes for description, refundability, grace period duration, and when they apply (immediately or delayed). The response can also include the client's current account balance and credit limit, allowing registrars to track their spending in real time.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask about create, renew, transfer, and the registry tells you the price for each one. It can also tell you when you get your money back and how much credit you have left.

sections.title: Fee Queries and Transform Commands
sections.content:
Transform commands (create, renew, delete, update, transfer) can include fee extension data. When a registrar submits a <create> command, it MAY include a <fee:create> element with the fees it expects to be charged. The server validates these fees against its own calculation: if the client's declared fees are less than the server's fees, the server rejects the command. If fees apply, the server MUST return a <fee:creData> response element showing the actual fees charged, the client's new balance (after the fee is deducted), and the credit limit.

The extension also adds elements to the <transfer> query command. When a registrar queries the status of an incoming transfer request, the server can include fee information for the gaining registrar (fees to acquire the domain) and the losing registrar (credits if applicable). The fee check command does not require client fees; the server provides what it would charge.
sections.plainLanguage: When you create a domain, you can say 'I expect to pay 5 dollars'. The registry checks: 'yes, that matches', or 'no, it is 10 dollars'. The registry always tells you what you actually owe.

sections.title: Currency Codes and Registration Periods
sections.content:
The extension uses three-character ISO 4217 currency codes (USD, EUR, GBP, etc.). Clients can specify a currency in fee check commands; if not, the server uses its default currency or the client's account settings. A special code, XXX, indicates a non-currency system such as credits or points. The fee response MUST include a currency element so the client knows which currency applies.

Registrars can specify how long they want to register or renew a domain using a <fee:period> element with a unit (years or months) and a value. For example, 2 years or 6 months. If no period is specified, the server uses its default. The server returns the period in its response so the registrar knows what interval the fees cover. The RFC states that fees apply to the total additional validity period for the object, so a fee for a 2-year period applies to the whole 2 years, not per year.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask in dollars, euros, or credits. You can ask about 1 year, 2 years, or 6 months. The registry tells you back in the same currency and period.

sections.title: Refunds, Grace Periods and Advanced Fees
sections.content:
Fees have an optional refundable attribute (true or false) indicating whether the registrar gets a refund if the domain is deleted. Many registries offer grace periods (defined in RFC 3915), typically 5 to 35 days after creation, renewal, or transfer, during which a delete refunds the fee. The fee element can carry a grace-period attribute as a duration (for example, P5D for 5 days).

The RFC requires that if a fee has a grace period, it MUST be refundable. Conversely, if a fee is not refundable, it MUST NOT have a grace period. Fees can also have an applied attribute marking them as immediate (deducted right away) or delayed (applied after an out-of-band process, such as reviewing applications at the end of a launch phase). If applied is delayed, the server's reported balance does not yet reflect the fee.
sections.plainLanguage: Some fees you get back if you delete the domain within a grace period, like 5 days. Some fees are charged right away, others only after the registry checks and approves your application.

sections.title: Security and Launch Phases
sections.content:
The fee extension passes financial information through EPP. Security depends entirely on the transport layer (TLS/SSL) and on the EPP protocol's authentication and authorization, as described in RFC 5730. The extension adds no new security services. The server MUST only provide fee information and account balance relevant to the authenticated client's account.

The extension supports launch phases for new domain extensions, defined in RFC 8334. A fee check can include phase and subphase attributes to request fees for specific launch phases (sunrise, landrush, general availability, claims, etc.). If a server has multiple active phases and the client does not specify one, the server rejects the command with a 'Required parameter missing' error. The RFC provides detailed rules for how servers must handle phase and subphase parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: Prices can be different during a domain extension's launch, like an early 'sunrise' period or later 'general availability'. The registrar can ask about fees in each phase.
